title: Nubbin and the Not-So-Neat Plan
markdown:
The Whispering Peaks were a topsy-turvy land of sharp summits and soft cloud-meadows. Ferry ropes, like long creaky sighs, stretched between them. Witch Tilda lived there, brewing starlight into tea and darning thunderclouds with needle and thread. Her best friend was Nubbin, a hedgehog whose prickles held more good sense than most folk’s entire heads. Usually.

One crisp morning Tilda needed to deliver a Potion of Perfect Pondering to Mayor Grumbles on the next peak before sundown. It was for the annual Whispering Peaks Debate, a time for the most serious of discussions.

“Come along, Nubbin, my dear! The sun’s already halfway up the sky. Mayor Grumbles will be pondering without his potion.”

Nubbin, usually as punctual as a mountain sunrise, was nowhere. Tilda searched under toadstools and behind whispering ferns. She found him wedged firmly, stubbornly, immovably, in the entrance to his favourite den. Little paws splayed. Nose tucked. The den felt safe. The world outside felt loud.

“Oh, Nubbin. Not now. We cannot possibly be heroically stubborn at precisely the wrong moment. The debate depends on this.”

He squeezed his eyes shut. Prickles bristled. His safe spot. Everything else too wobbly.

The ground rumbled. Ogre Mallow strode past, boots like small craters, beard like spun moonlight, a neat tidy plan for everything. “Tilda, my dear! Trouble with the little spiky one?” Nubbin was stuck tighter than a pebble in a plum. “The best way to move a stubborn creature is a series of precisely placed nudges, followed by a carefully calculated push. Like so!”

Before he could nudge, wind whipped past, pine sap and worried rock-wrens. The sun dipped. Long shadows. Tilda’s stomach fluttered; she did not name the feeling. She watched the light instead.

Then a flash. Inigo Bafflegab, a weasel who could talk the spots off a ladybug, squawked, “Aha! The obvious solution! But the truly clever way is always the most elaborate. A contraption! A pulley system!” He pointed at a gnarled oak and a wispy vine. “The neatest-looking plan. Surely the cleverest.”

Mallow’s plan was neat. Inigo’s was elaborate. Nubbin remained a statue of determination.

Listen to the stubborn, Tilda’s grandmother had said. They often know what the earth knows.

“Sometimes the neatest plan isn’t the one that gets you where you need to go,” Tilda murmured, fingers on her spellbook. “It’s the one that listens.” Nubbin wiggled one tiny determined foot. Trying.

“Perhaps a different approach.” She knelt. “What is it, little friend? What are you trying to tell me?” He huffed and pointed his nose at a small moss-covered crevice, usually overlooked.

The crevice led to a narrow winding tunnel. Not neat. Not elaborate. Different. A gentle word, a tiny puff of wind-magic that tickled his ears, and Nubbin shuffled, then slid through, out of Mallow’s nudging range and Inigo’s ambitious pulley.

“Well, I never!” Mallow boomed. “That was not in my calculations.”

“A mere detour!” sniffed Inigo, already inventing a more complex contraption.

Tilda saw. Nubbin had not been stubborn for no reason. He had been following a way that felt right to hedgehog senses. Listen to the stubborn.

The tunnel smelled of damp earth and ancient secrets. Nubbin scurried. Prickles rustled. Tilda followed, heart lighter. They emerged into a hidden grotto, ethereal light, a crystal-clear mountain pool. A secret the mountains kept.

Inigo’s vine contraption was almost there, a triumphant squeak echoing. Mallow was still calculating the angle of his next nudge on a boulder.

Ahead, a narrow ledge, a ribbon of rock. The ferry rope to Mayor Grumbles’ peak swayed in the buffeting wind.

“See!” Inigo crowed. “My neat elaborate plan is the fastest. The most reliable.”

He stepped onto the vine. A loose stone tumbled, struck with a sharp TWANG. The vine snapped. Inigo yelped, dangling over the chasm.

Mallow abandoned his nudging. “Highly inefficient! We must secure him. Quickly.” Large rocks. A sturdy mushroom.

The sun sank fast. Nubbin refused the swaying ferry rope. He dug his paws in, a solid anchor against howling wind.

“Oh, for goodness sake, Nubbin. We can’t stop now.” Then Tilda looked. He was staring at the rope, then the crumbling cliff. Sensing.

“We cannot possibly panic yet,” Mallow said, surveying dangling Inigo. “We have not even had tea. Efficiency requires proper sustenance.”

Inigo’s plan had failed because it was too complicated. Mallow’s was too slow. Nubbin’s instincts were screaming. Listen to the stubborn.

Tilda breathed. “You’re right. That rope isn’t safe.” The cliff was loose and treacherous, but there were tiny handholds, rough patches, places where determination could find purchase. Nubbin’s way.

She loosened the Potion of Perfect Pondering and sprinkled a tiny shimmering drop on his prickles. Not to change him. To help his sensible stubbornness shine.

Nubbin scrambled up the crumbling face. Wind shrieked. Grit scraped Tilda’s palms. Ancient rock in her lungs. He did not sprint. Careful steps, prickles in crevices, paws scrabbling. She followed. Hard work. A tiny determined pioneer.

They reached the top just as Inigo was being awkwardly lowered by Mallow, who had wisely decided a cup of strong mountain tea might be the most efficient next step.

The ferry rope still swayed, a wild pendulum. Nubbin nudged her forward. No longer stubbornly stuck. Stubbornly brave.

Together they crossed, hearts thumping against the wind, and landed with a relieved thump on Mayor Grumbles’ peak as the last sun vanished. The debate was saved. The potion had arrived.

Tilda hugged him, careful of prickles, feeling solid warmth. She did not call his stubbornness a flaw, or a lecture. She held him. Nubbin gave a contented huff. He had insisted on his way. Listen to the stubborn. That was the way that mattered.
characters: Tilda (starlight witch), Nubbin (a stubborn hedgehog), Mallow (a tidy ogre)
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
